summary:
Niels Rogge, on Hugging Face's community science team, automates outreach that nudges researchers to publish weights and data sets on the Hub instead of Google Drive, Dropbox, Zenodo, or GitHub releases. With hundreds of arXiv papers daily, manual templated GitHub issues and pull requests were unsustainable.

His first system replicates the original manual path as a deterministic workflow of LLM API calls with no agent framework, running nightly as a Python cron job on free GitHub Actions minutes, traced with LangFuse for prompts, cost, and latency. It produces hundreds of GitHub issues per night.

Because replies accumulated faster than he could answer, he rebuilt the follow-up half as a fully autonomous Claude Agent SDK loop. Its main tool is bash plus the Hugging Face CLI skill, with Slack visibility. He invokes it manually from Cursor as a "process under it Modal" skill that runs Composer 2.5 and fans out one container per issue via Modal's batch processing. The model was recently switched from Claude to GLM 5.2 via Hugging Face inference providers.

He does not disclose that recipients are talking to an agent, reasoning that disclosed bots get closed unread while the agent sends what he used to send himself. Out of thousands of issues, he recalls only two negative replies, with examples ranging from an Apple researcher DMed about a new Apple paper to Paddle OCR migrating all OCR models. To avoid slop, he recommends Hamel Husain's LLM Evils FAQ. He concludes open models like GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 now rival closed ones, agents beat workflows for his case, and evaluation matters. He closes with adjacent efforts: a Daily Papers Twitter account crossing 90,000 followers and a revival of Papers With Code at paperswithcode.co.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Google Drive to the hub problem
sections.summary: Niels introduces himself as a five-year ML engineer on Hugging Face's community science team, framed as the 'Google Drive to the hub' team that nudges researchers to publish artifacts on the Hub instead of third-party services.

sections.title: Paper pages, metadata, and discoverability
sections.summary: He explains how Hugging Face paper pages link models and data sets, with metadata tags filtering by task, library, and language to improve discoverability, framing a win-win for researchers and users.

sections.title: Why manual outreach does not scale
sections.summary: He describes the templated GitHub issues and PRs he opened by hand, then notes that hundreds of new arXiv papers daily, plus surges like NeurIPS and the AI boom, make this manual work unsustainable.

sections.title: The workflow he was running by hand
sections.summary: He lays out the five-step manual path to automate: find GitHub URL, read README, decide if anything new should be shared, open a PR if cards or tags are missing on existing artifacts, otherwise open a GitHub issue, then follow up.

sections.title: Workflow or agent, and why it is not binary
sections.summary: Using Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' framing, he contrasts deterministic workflows with fully autonomous agents, notes they can mix, and explains choosing a deterministic workflow because Anthropic advised avoiding agents and frameworks when not needed.

sections.title: Nightly cron jobs, and tracing cost and latency
sections.summary: The workflow is a nightly Python cron job running on free GitHub Actions minutes, producing hundreds of GitHub issues per night, with LangFuse used to trace prompts, inputs, outputs, cost, and latency.

sections.title: The flood of replies, and automating follow up
sections.summary: He notes the unread GitHub notifications from nightly issues and frames the question of whether to also automate the follow-up loop, initially still doing it himself.

sections.title: Switching to a fully autonomous loop
sections.summary: Citing Anthropic's AI Engineer workshop claim that agents now beat workflows and Cursor's talk about replacing 12,000 lines with a 200-line skill, he rebuilds the follow-up half as a Claude Agent SDK loop.

sections.title: Bash, one CLI, one skill, one sandbox
sections.summary: He details the architecture: Claude Agent SDK plus bash as the main tool, the Hugging Face CLI skill for HF commands, GitHub comments for follow-up, and Slack posting for visibility, with a recent switch from Claude to GLM 5.2 via Hugging Face inference providers.

sections.title: A container per issue, fanned out
sections.summary: He explains deploying on Modal using its batch processing to spin up many containers in parallel, each handling one GitHub issue, with fast startups suitable for overnight background agents.

sections.title: Invoking the follow-up loop from Cursor
sections.summary: He describes manually invoking the follow-up loop from Cursor via a 'process under it Modal' skill that runs Composer 2.5 and posts all results to the team's Slack channel, with the skill still triggered manually.

sections.title: Fun results: replies, DMs, and migrations
sections.summary: He shares positive outcomes including Apple researchers DMing him about a new Apple paper, Google DeepMind outreach for math data sets, a 400 GB data set migration request, and Paddle OCR migrating all OCR models after agent outreach.

sections.title: Model card completion and the slop problem
sections.summary: He shows the agent completing default Hugging Face model card templates from paper, README, and PDF content, sometimes crediting him as a model card author without prompting, then warns about slop and recommends Hamel Husain's LLM Evils FAQ.

sections.title: Conclusion: open models, agents over workflows, evaluation
sections.summary: He concludes that open models like GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 now rival closed ones, agents beat workflows for his use case given one CLI, one skill, and a sandbox, and evaluation should not be forgotten.

sections.title: Adjacent efforts: Daily Papers and Papers With Code revival
sections.summary: He briefly showcases his Daily Papers Twitter account that has crossed 90,000 followers using the same workflow plus Gemini-chosen visuals, and his revival of Papers With Code at paperswithcode.co as both a benchmark and educational resource.
